summary: Specifies a data model for configuring and monitoring IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) and Packet Sampling (PSAMP) devices using NETCONF. It covers selection processes, caches, exporting processes, and collecting processes. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Network devices that count traffic need a control panel. This memo defines a standard panel, with named switches and dials, to set up how they count and where they send results.

subtitle: A vendor-neutral, NETCONF-ready configuration model for devices that measure and export IP traffic flows and sampled packets.

tldr.problem: IPFIX and PSAMP devices from different makers each had their own way of being configured, which made managing a mixed network harder.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6728 defines a configuration and state data model drawn as UML classes and written formally in YANG, covering Observation Points, Selection Processes, Caches, Exporting Processes and Collecting Processes. The configuration data is encoded in XML for use with NETCONF.
tldr.outcome: Devices can announce which parts of the model they support through YANG features and deviations, so one model fits many implementations. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6728 is a Proposed Standard from October 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its module is registered as ietf-ipfix-psamp with the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ipfix-psamp.

sections.title: Why a Common Configuration Model
sections.content:
IPFIX- and PSAMP-compliant Monitoring Devices (routers, switches, monitoring probes, Collectors and so on) offer many configuration choices, so monitoring can be adapted to accounting, traffic analysis, performance monitoring or security monitoring. A common, vendor-independent model helps when devices from different manufacturers are deployed together. It also lets the configuration be stored in a consistent format and used for local and remote configuration.

The model covers the commonly available parameters of Selection Processes, Caches, Exporting Processes and Collecting Processes, plus some common state parameters. It is drawn with UML class diagrams, and an XML document conforming to it holds the configuration data of one Monitoring Device. It is designed for the NETCONF protocol (RFC 6241), and YANG (RFC 6020) is used to specify it formally.
sections.eli5: Imagine every brand of toaster had different knobs. This memo says all traffic-counting devices should use the same knobs.

sections.title: Selection Process, Cache and Export
sections.content:
The model splits the Metering Process into two blocks. A Selection Process takes the Observed Packet Stream and picks a subset, the Selected Packet Stream, using one Selector (a Primitive Selector) or an ordered list of them (a Composite Selector). A Cache then builds IPFIX Flow Records or PSAMP Packet Reports from that stream. The model does not allow a Cache with no Selection Process in front of it. To keep every packet, you configure a Selector of the SelectAll class.

For an Exporter the chain is: ObservationPoint, then SelectionProcess, then Cache, then ExportingProcess. Several Observation Points can feed one Selection Process, and several Selection Processes can feed one Cache. A Cache MUST NOT aggregate packets from different Observation Domains in the same Flow. A Collector is configured with a CollectingProcess, which can point at ExportingProcess objects to reexport what it receives, for instance to a File Writer.

If a reference in the chain is missing, the output is dropped. Such configurations are incomplete but not invalid, since they may exist while a device is being configured in steps.
sections.eli5: Think of a sorting line at a factory. First a worker picks which items to look at, then another writes them in a log, then a third mails the log to the office.

sections.title: How the Model Is Written
sections.content:
Each class becomes an XML element, with the first letter lowercase. Its attributes are configuration or state parameters. A multiplicity such as [0..1] marks an optional parameter, [0..*] one that may repeat, and [1..*] one that MUST be given at least once. An attribute with a default, such as ipfixVersion = 10, uses that default if you do not configure it. Attributes with no marker and no default are mandatory.

Two further properties matter. {opt.} means you MAY configure the parameter, but if you do not, the device MUST pick a value and not change it afterwards. {readOnly} marks state parameters that cannot be configured, such as counters.

Classes relate by aggregation (nested XML) or by unidirectional association (a reference by name). Classes with configuration parameters that can occur many times need a key called name, unique within its subtree, because YANG requires keys for list entries.
sections.eli5: Each setting is a labeled form field. Some you must fill in, some are optional, and some are just meters you can look at but not change.

sections.title: Selectors and Caches
sections.content:
An ObservationPoint says where packets are seen: interfaces or physical entities such as linecards, identified by name or by index, and a direction of ingress, egress or both (the default). Its observationDomainId groups points into an Observation Domain.

A Selector holds exactly one method: SelectAll, count-based, time-based, random n-out-of-N or uniform probabilistic Sampling, or property match or hash Filtering, matching the functions of RFC 6727. It also carries counters such as packetsObserved and packetsDropped. Hash filters default to the BOB function, a payload offset of 0 and a payload size of 8. Time parameters are in microseconds, and the uniform probability is a value between 0 and 1.

The Cache type decides what comes out. ImmediateCache makes a Packet Report for each packet. The other three make Flow Records and differ in when Flows expire. A CacheLayout lists the Information Elements to include, and each field can be marked as a Flow Key.
sections.eli5: You choose where to watch, how to pick what to look at, and how to write it down. Each choice has its own small settings card.

sections.title: Exporting and Collecting
sections.content:
An ExportingProcess has one or more Destinations, each using an SctpExporter, UdpExporter, TcpExporter or FileWriter. The default ipfixVersion is 10. The default destination port is 4739 without TLS or DTLS and 4740 with it. The exportMode decides how Data Records go to the destinations, and the default is parallel.

An Options object chooses which extra information to report with Options Templates, such as Metering Process statistics or the Flow Key specification. A CollectingProcess sets the local addresses, transports and ports, or acts as a File Reader. The model also includes a Template class holding state data for the Templates a transport session uses.
sections.eli5: The sender can mail its reports to many addresses at once, take turns between them, or try a backup address if the first fails.

sections.title: TLS and DTLS Settings
sections.content:
A TransportLayerSecurity object enables TLS or DTLS. DTLS is used when the transport is SCTP or UDP, and TLS when it is TCP. An empty <transportLayerSecurity /> element turns it on with no further parameters. RFC 5101 requires strong mutual authentication of Exporting and Collecting Processes, using X.509 certificates matched to the peer's fully qualified domain name (FQDN).

The model lets you limit trusted remote endpoints to specific certification authorities or FQDNs, and limit which local certificate is used when a device has several. For security reasons it offers no way to upload certificates or keys. If TLS or DTLS is enabled on a device without suitable ones, the configuration MUST be rejected with an error.
sections.eli5: Before two devices swap reports they show each other ID cards. The model lets you say which ID cards you will accept.

sections.title: Fitting Real Devices
sections.content:
The model is a superset of common parameters, and few devices support all of it. YANG features make parts conditional. The exporter, collector and meter features gate whole blocks, and further features cover each sampling and filtering method, each Cache type, UDP and TCP transport, and the File Reader and File Writer.

Deviations let a device state limits on existing parameters, such as a narrower value range. Model extensions use YANG's augment statement to add new parameters. Constraints YANG cannot express MUST be given in human-readable description text. A device MUST notify the user of any configuration it cannot support and MUST NOT silently accept configuration data it cannot enforce.
sections.eli5: Not every device can do everything on the list, so each one tells you which parts it has, and complains if you ask for something it cannot do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG module is meant to be accessed over NETCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH (RFC 6242). Writable nodes can be sensitive. Write access to /ipfix/observationPoint or /ipfix/selectionProcess could lead to export of sensitive traffic information, and write access to /ipfix/cache could add fields such as IP addresses or parts of the payload.

Write access to /ipfix/exportingProcess could send data to illegitimate Collectors or change the TLS/DTLS parameters that protect it. Write access to /ipfix/collectingProcess could cause reexport or storage of the data. Readable nodes may also be sensitive, since they reveal infrastructure details, observed-traffic counters, and Collector or Exporter addresses together with TLS/DTLS settings. Read access should be controlled too.
sections.eli5: Whoever can change these settings can point the reports at the wrong place, so only trusted people should hold the keys.

items.label: Parallel
items.desc: Every Data Record goes to all configured destinations.

items.label: Load balancing
items.desc: Each record goes to exactly one destination, chosen by a device-specific policy.

items.label: Fallback
items.desc: Each record goes to one destination; the next one is tried if the previous fails.
